i thought I would write this post to try and bring a little sanity to the gun buying world. There are currently more riles and calibers than you could spend a day at a keyboard listing.

With so many different rifles and calibers we should probably change our perspective. Ask your self "Why am I buying this particular rifle in this particular caliber"?

Now I know there is the collector class that buy rifles because they want one of each type.

But for most of us ( with a limited budget and family responsibilities) the wanting to buy a rifle is driven more by need.

Now why do I need a rifle?

Only three good reasons: (1) self protection; (2) put meat on the table: (3) eliminate pests that eat up my garden or kill my livestock.

So with the above reasons listed , we could reasonably be expected to purchase three different rifles.

  1. For self protection, that practically mandates a high capacity, ease of use, reliable. rapid fire rifle with enough power to get the job done with out going into over kill. Did I mention recoil. Well no I didn't but I should. A rifle that has the above three attributes but kicks like a Missouri mule is out of the question if you expect the little woman (read wife here) to have to use it to defend the kith and kinder. I have have posted in other places SIR, ISSAC NEWTON is the bitch god of the universe. Large caliber bullets flying at high velocity means the rifle is going to come back at you with great force.

  2. Putting meat on the table. This requirement has a lot more complications than self-protection. First of all in modern day America we aren't going to starve to death if we can't bag dinner. So putting meat on the table is more of an exercise of entertainment than a necessity. But still the same principles apply. The rifle must be reasonably accurate, easy to use, have enough power to put the animal down with out two much trouble even with less than perfect bullet placement, light enough to carry for a long period, reliable, with sufficient range to match the capabilities of the shooter. In a hunting rifle high ammo capacity is really a determent as ammo is heavy and the ability to carry the rifle for long distances out weighs the ability to carry 30 rounds in the magazine. In a hunting rifle the rate of fire is irreverent if all you need is one or two shots. (You do know that double rifles are still being made?) In a hunting rifle recoil is of less importance as the rifle will be fired only one or two times during the event. Lastly in the hunting category the rifle should match the game being taken. The rifle that is adequate to take down a white tail buck is not adequate for taking down a Rocky Mountain Elk, a Moose are a BROWN BEAR. The minimum cartridge for a Elk is a .270 and that is marginal, and I don't give a shit what the late Jack O'Connor, the Shooting Editor of Outdoor Life wrote. He got a way with all the things he wrote about because he was a expert shot and a hunter par excellence who spent all his time hunting. For the rest of us Mortals the minimum rifle for taking game with a body weight of 600 lbs or greater should be a 7.5 mm or greater. Lastly if you are going after BROWN BEAR You better have a .300 mag or better or have your life insurance policy up to date.

  3. Shooting of pests. (Commonly known as Varmint hunting) Now since most of us don't have vast acreages filled with crops and live stock but have a few tomato and rose bushes in the back yard, that we would like to keep the crows and deer out of means an entirely different approach to weapon buying. Living in the city or the burbs if you light off any kind of fire arm you are going to get a visit by the local constabulary, which is something none of us want. We will not mention that shooting Mr. Bucky as he nibbles on MiLady's rose bushes, could raise the ire of the animal rights crowd, and the state fish and game commission. So for this kind of pest control a modern precision air rifle should do the trick. Modern air rifles are not the trusty Daisy bee bee guns of old. They are precision tools made to put a projectile on target at 10 meters. (32.8 feet) You can get a pretty good air rifle for about a bill and a half. ($150.00) that you can shoot all day in your back yard and not attract that much attention. Also the principles involved in shooting a modern air rifle are the same in shooting any rifle. Lastly the ammo you need for a Air Rifle is dirt cheap and will last forever. (Amazone has (500) .22 cal air rifle pellets for $6.47.

For those of us in live in more rural areas we can have a modern .22 cal rimfire. The only problem with the trusty .22 is they are a* fire arm and are lethal if handled carelessly*. Most .22 cal rifles today are not all that expensive. Most are high capacity, easy to use, rapid firing and reasonably accurate. While they are quite useful in dispatching Mr. Dirty Rat, Mr. Ground Squirrel and Mr. Squawking Crow I would not recommend you using it on Mr, Bucky nibbling on Milady's rose bushes, as again the animal rights crowd and the State Fish and Game commission will get annoyed. For us purests who insist on taking pests at over two hundred yds or for those who live in Texas where the largest pest is the feral hog (every thing is Texas is bigger don't you know), something a little more powerful than the .22 cal rimfire is necessary. This field is wide open with a lot of cross over between the self protection firearm and the hunting fire arm. The only requirement is that it will be by definition a center-fire cartridge of 5mm or larger. I would say that the upper limit for a varmint rifle would be about 6.5mm as anything larger will be too expensive, and not to mention punishing recoil. to blast away with for a long duration. Also on a long range pest control rifle the purchase of good optics is mandatory. Good optics as a rule of thumb should be one half the price of the rifle.

Any why the above are my opinions and there are many who would argue finer points as "what about my SMALLEBODEDENLOUDENBOOMER"
